INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE
The American Civil Liberties Union
(“ACLU”) is a nationwide, nonprofit organization
that has sought to defend and advance  civil liberties
in the United States  since 1920 . The ACLU of the
District of Columbia and the ACLU of Hawai‘i are
two of the ACLU’s affiliates . The ACLU  frequently
appears in this Court, as counsel  for parties and as
amicus curiae, in cases concerning government
accountability for violations of individuals’ rights and
liberties, including in Bivens cases. See, e.g., Egbert v.
Boule, 596 U.S. 482 (2022)  (amicus); Hernández v.
Mesa, 589 U.S. 93 (2020)  (amicus); Bivens v. Six
Unknown Named Agents of the Fed. Bur. of Narcotics,
403 U.S. 388 (1971) (amicus).1
INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF
ARGUMENT
Kekai Watanabe was brutally attacked in a prison
fight and his tailbone was broken. For months, prison
staff denied his requests for hospital care, providing
him instead with over -the-counter pain medication .
Mr. Watanabe now seeks to bring a damages claim for
his months of pain and suffering. Doing so is his only
way to hold accountable the officials who ignored his
repeated requests for care. Under a straightforward

1 Pursuant to Supreme Court Rule 37.6, counsel for amici certify

fund the preparation or submission of the brief; and no person

2
application of Carlson v. Green, 446 U.S. 14 (1980), he
states a viable claim.
Carlson relied on Bivens v. Six Unknown Named
Agents, 403 U.S. 388 (1971), to infer a damages
remedy for “a federal prisoner’s inadequate-care claim
under the Eighth Amendment .” Egbert v. Boule, 596
U.S. 482, 490 –91 (2022). Eight years after Carlson,
Congress passed the Westfall Act, which exempted all
civil actions “brought for a violation of the
Constitution of the United States ” from the Act’s
remedial exclusivity provisions.  28 U.S.C.
§ 2679(b)(2)(A); see also Hui v. Castaneda , 559 U.S.
799, 807 (2010) . As this Court has repeatedly
recognized, that exemption was Congress’s way of
“expressly . . . preserving . . . liability for Bivens
actions,” United States v. Smith , 499 U.S. 160, 173
(1991)—ensuring, in other words, that the Westfall
Act “left Bivens where it found it,” Hernández v. Mesa,
589 U.S. 93, 111 n.9 (2020).
Congress’s decision to safeguard Bivens liability
must be respected. Although inferring causes of action
is now “a disfavored judicial activity,” Ziglar v.
Abbasi, 582 U.S. 120, 135 (2017)  (citation modified),
the Westfall Act endorsed Bivens as it stood in 1988.
That endorsement should inform how the Court
approaches Carlson in this case . At the time of the
Westfall Act’s passage, courts applied Carlson to any
Eighth Amendment claim alleging unconstitutionally
deficient prison medical care —not just cases
presenting precisely the same facts as Carlson.
Because Congress relied upon that judicial
understanding when it passed the Westfall Act, the
Court cannot now reduce Carlson to its facts. Instead,

3
to respect the work of Congress, the “context” inquiry
must pay just as much heed to what Congress has
authorized as to what it has not. Concretely, then, just
as the Court has declined, in all of its post-1988 Bivens
cases through the present, to extend Bivens to novel
circumstances Congress could not have authorized in
1988, the Court should not hesitate to permit Bivens
applications that were well settled when Congress
acted in 1988. Failing to do so would be just as much
an “arrogati[on of] legislative power” as extending
Bivens liability to novel circumstances Congress has
left unaddressed. Hernández, 589 U.S. at 100.
Longstanding principles of statutory
interpretation support construing the scope of Carlson
as Congress would have in 1988. When Congress
legislates about a well -established legal concept, the
prior construction canon presumes that Congress
intended to incorporate that established meaning, as
reflected both in the decisions of this Court and in any
broad consensus among appellate courts. See, e.g.,
Lamar, Archer & Cofrin, LLP v. Appling , 584 U.S.
709, 721 (2018) . Th is rule is rooted in a core
separation-of-powers principle : “It is just as much
‘judicial legislation’ for a court to withdraw a remedy
which Congress expected to be continued as to
improvise one that Congress never had in mind.”
Merrill Lynch, Pierce, Fenner & Smith, Inc. v. Curran,
456 U.S. 353, 394 n.100 (1982) (citation modified); see
also Franklin v. Gwinnett Cnty. Pub. Schs. , 503 U.S.
60, 74 (1992) (explaining that failing to enforce a valid
cause of action “would harm separation of powers
principles . . . by giving judges the power to render

4
inutile causes of action authorized by Congress
through a decision that no remedy is available”).
By contrast, Petitioner’s and the United States’
demand for precise factual symmetry between
Carlson and all subsequent Eighth Amendment
damages claims about inadequate prison medical care
cannot be squared with the Westfall Act’s text. The
provision preserving Bivens liability is exception-free:
nowhere does it identify or discuss the factual
scenarios of the Bivens cases the Court decided prior
to 1988. To insist now that the provision preserves
only claims that duplicate the facts of those cases—
rather than the principles on which those cases were
decided—is a willful misreading of Congress’s
directive. Under Petitioner’ s artificial congruence
rule, Carlson would apply not to “Eighth Amendment
prison medical care  claims” but only to “Eighth
Amendment claims of incarcerated asthmatics who
died as a result of deficient medical care.” Neither the
Westfall Act nor a logical system of precedent works
this way. See Epic Sys. Corp. v. Lewis , 584 U.S. 497,
510 (2018).
Petitioner’s argument that the Administrative
Remedy Program (“ARP”) renders every prison claim
sui generis —along with the United States’ corollary
admission that “no more Carlson claims will be viable”
under this approach, Amicus Br. for U.S. 3—invites an
even greater usurpation of legislative power.
Petitioner and the United States effectively ask this
Court to take a red pen to the Westfall Act and scratch
out a whole category of Bivens applications. But that
category indisputably existed when Congress acted to
preserve that remedy. To bar such claims today

5
because of the ARP would “retroactively impose” on
Congress a “new presumption” that “did not exist at
the time of enactment” of the Westfall Act. Tanzin v.
Tanvir, 592 U.S. 43, 52 (2020) . The separation of
powers forbids this outcome.
While minimizing or even rewriting the Westfall
Act, Petitioner and the United States urge the Court
to focus on more general statutes about procedures for
prison claims (chiefly, the Prison Litigation Reform
Act). In fact, these laws can easily be harmonized with
the Westfall Act, and separation-of-powers principles
demand that this Court do so. The Westfall Act
preserves the Bivens cause of action as Congress found
it in 1988  (including well-recognized applications of
Carlson). Meanwhile, Congress’s other, more general
laws impose procedural limitations and provide other
safeguards that coexist with—but do not eliminate or
diminish—Carlson claims. These statutes work
together, not against one another.  The Court should
reject the invitation of Petitioner and the United
States to turn statutory interpretation into “an
exercise in looking over a crowd and picking out your
friends.” Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Allapattah Servs., Inc.,
545 U.S. 546, 568 (2005) (citation modified).
Congress has done the hard work , so t he
separation of powers makes this case an easy one.
When Congress passed the Westfall Act, it endorsed
what this Court and the circuits understood Carlson
to stand for  at the time : the general availability of a
damages action for a “federal prisoner’s inadequate -
care claim under the Eighth Amendment.” Egbert, 596
U.S. at 490–91. That availability did not turn on how
closely the facts of any given claim resembled those in

6
Carlson. Abiding by Congress’s decision now means
preserving Carlson as it stood in 1988.  Because
Congress blessed the general availability of Eighth
Amendment Bivens claims for unconstitutionally
deficient prison medical care , claims like Mr.
Watanabe’s must be allowed to proceed.
The judgment below should be affirmed.
ARGUMENT
I. THE CARLSON “CONTEXT” INCLUDES
WHAT CONGRESS ENDORSED IN THE
WESTFALL ACT.
The Court has prescribed a two -step test for
determining when a Bivens cause of action is
available. First, courts must assess whether the claim
arises in a “new context.” Abbasi, 582 U.S. at 139. If a
claim falls within an existing Bivens “context”—that
is, if it isn’t “meaningfully different from the three
cases in which the Court has implied a damages
action”—a Bivens action is available and the claim
may proceed. Egbert, 596 U.S. at 492 (citation
modified). If a claim does raise a “new context,” courts
continue to the second step, at which they consider
any “special factors counselling hesitation in the
absence of affirmative action by Congress.” Abbasi,
582 U.S. at 136, 139–40; accord Hernández, 589 U.S.
at 102. “If there is even a single reason to pause before
applying Bivens in a new context, a court may not
recognize a Bivens remedy.” Egbert, 596 U.S. at 492
(citation modified).
This case turns on the first of the two questions:
Is the “context” here a “new” one? More specifically, is

7
there a “meaningful[] differen[ce]” between Carlson,
which recognized a Bivens action for a “ federal
prisoner’s inadequate -care claim under the Eighth
Amendment” Egbert, 596 U.S. at 490 –91, based on
prison officials ’ failure to provide adequate medical
care after he suffered an asthma attack , and Mr.
Watanabe’s claim, which is about  prison officials’
failure to provide adequate medical care for his broken
tailbone?
Congress has already answered this question . In
the Federal Employees Liability Reform and Tort
Compensation Act of 1988 (commonly known as the
“Westfall Act”), Congress made the Federal Tort
Claims Act (“FTCA”)  the “exclusive” remedy for
injuries resulting from the conduct of federal
employees acting within the scope of their
employment. See 28 U.S.C. §  2679(b)(1). The
exclusivity provision has, as relevant here , a critical
exception: it “does not extend or apply to a civil action
against an employee of the Government  . . . which is
brought for a violation of the Constitution of the
United States.” Id. § 2679(b)(2)(A). As this Court has
explained, Congress inserted th is savings clause
“expressly” to “preserv[e] employee liability for Bivens
actions.” United States v. Smith , 499 U.S. 160, 173
(1991). In doing so, Congress “reli[ed] upon [Bivens] as
a fixed principle in the law.” Abbasi, 582 U.S. at 134.
Congress’s decision to preserve Bivens liability
dictates how far the Carlson “context” now extends.
When Congress passed the Westfall Act, courts would
have found no meaningful difference between Carlson
and claims like Mr. Watanabe’s: C ourts construed
Carlson to cover Eighth Amendment claims for

8
inadequate prison medical care generally. That
understanding matters today because where Congress
incorporates “a judicially defined concept” such as
Bivens into legislation, courts should “ presume[],
absent an express statement to the contrary, that
Congress intended to adopt the interpretation placed
on that concept by the courts.” Davis v. Mich. Dep’t of
Treasury, 489 U.S. 803, 813 (1989) . When Congress
ensured Bivens liability survived via the Westfall Act,
it “adopt[ed]” courts’ understanding of Carlson at the
time. Congress’s choice to endorse courts’ broad view
of Carlson as of 1988 determines when a claim
“meaningfully differ[s]” from Carlson now. Egbert, 596
U.S. at 492.
A. The Prior Construction Canon Applies to
the Westfall Act’s Savings Clause.
The prior construction canon directs courts to
“assume that, when Congress enacts statutes, it is
aware of relevant judicial precedent.” Merck & Co. v.
Reynolds, 559 U.S. 633, 648 (2010) ; accord, e.g., Atl.
Sounding Co., Inc. v. Townsend , 557 U.S. 404, 422
(2009). More specifically, “The normal rule of
statutory construction is that if Congress intends for
legislation to change the interpretation of a judicially
created concept, it makes that intent specific.”
Midlantic Nat’l Bank v. N.J. Dep’t of Environmental
Prot., 474 U.S. 494, 501 (1986); accord, e.g., Unicolors,
Inc. v. H&M Hennes & Mauritz, L.P. , 595 U.S. 178,
186 (2022); Davis, 489 U.S. at 813 (1989).
Applying this principle, the Court has repeatedly
held that Congress legislates against the backdrop of
relevant precedent and incorporates the

9
understandings of those cases it does not overrule.
See, e.g., Tanzin, 592 U.S. at 48 –50; Merck, 559 U.S.
at 648; Gomez-Perez v. Potter , 553 U.S. 474, 484 –85
(2008); Jackson v. Birmingham Bd. of Educ., 544 U.S.
167, 176–77 (2005); Miles v. Apex Marine Corp. , 498
U.S. 19, 32 (1990).
Lower court decisions, in addition to those of this
Court, matter for the prior construction canon . How
the “Courts of Appeals [have] consistently construed”
the relevant concepts  can form part of the settled
judicial understanding that the principle recognizes ,
Lamar, Archer & Cofrin, LLP v. Appling , 584 U.S.
709, 721 (2018) , so long as there is  a “broad and
unquestioned consensus”  among the lower courts,
Trump v. Cook, 146 S. Ct. 2234, 2253 (2026)  (citation
modified). Thus, this Court has repeatedly interpreted
statutes by reference to  the consensus of appellate
case law at the time of the statute’s passage. See, e.g.,
Unicolors, 595 U.S. at 186; Lamar, Archer, 584 U.S. at
721–22 & n.3; Merck, 559 U.S. at 646–48.
The Court has applied the prior  construction
principle in cases like this one —namely, those
concerning the congressional endorsement  of
judicially recognized causes of action . In Merrill
Lynch, Pierce, Fenner & Smith, Inc. v. Curran , 456
U.S. 353 (1982), the Court held that Congress, in the
1974 amendments to the Commodity Exchange Act,
preserved an “implied private cause of action” that
“the federal courts routinely and consistently had
recognized” at that time . Id. at 379. The Court
reasoned that Congress’s enactment of a “saving
clause . . . provide[d] direct evidence of legislative
intent to preserve the implied private remedy federal

10
courts had recognized under the [Act].” Id. at 386. As
the Court stated the interpretive rule in Merrill
Lynch: “Congress need not have intended to create a
new remedy, since one already existed; the question is
whether Congress intended to preserve the pre -
existing remedy.” Id. at 378–79.
Moreover, the Court has applied the prior
construction canon to interpret congressional
directives as to the scope, not just the existence , of a
judicially inferred cause of action. And the Court has
done so even where it might have approached the
issue differently had it been writing on a blank slate.
In Franklin v. Gwinnett County Public Schools , 503
U.S. 60 (1992) , the Court considered whether a
plaintiff asserting the implied right of action for sex
discrimination that the Court recognized in Cannon v.
University of Chicago, 441 U.S. 677 (1979), could seek
damages. The Court unanimously held that she could,
in significant part because Congress, after Cannon,
enacted a statute clearly indicat ing that damages
should be available. See Franklin, 503 U.S. at 72 –73
(discussing the Rehabilitation Act Amendments of
1986). The Court concluded that Congress had
endorsed the judicially created remedy and recognized
the availability of damages , even though it had not
explicitly codified the right of action that the Court
had inferred or explicitly provided for damages. See id.
Even Justices who questioned the propriety of
judicially inferred causes of action nonetheless
concluded that Congress’s ratification of the remedy
was dispositive . In a concurrence joined by Chief
Justice Rehnquist and Justice Thomas, Justice Scalia
noted:

11
Because of legislation enacted subsequent to
Cannon, it is too late in the day to address
whether a judicially implied exclusion of
damages under Title IX would be appropriate.
The Rehabilitation Act Amendments of 1986
must be read, in my view, not only “as a
validation of Cannon’s holding,” but also as an
implicit acknowledgment that damages are
available.
Id. at 78 (Scalia, J., concurring in judgment) (citation
modified); accord Alexander v. Sandoval , 532 U.S.
275, 280 (2001) (citing this analysis approvingly). And
more recently this  Court has reaffirmed Franklin’s
recognition that Congress ratified the holding of
Cannon, despite the Court ’s “retreat[]” from other
aspects of Cannon’s reasoning . Medina v. Planned
Parenthood S. Atl. , 606 U.S. 357, 369 n.1 (2025)
(citation modified).
Petitioner says very little about the Westfall Act
and nothing at all about the prior construction canon.
On the Westfall Act, Petitioner claims that Congress’s
reliance on Carlson in 1988 “is precisely the problem.”
Pet’r’s Br. 47 ( citation modified ). According to
Petitioner, Congress’s decision to endorse Carlson in
the Westfall Act is an example of  courts providing
Congress with “an excuse not to” “legislate.” Id.
But Congress’s preservation of  Carlson in the
Westfall Act is not a “problem” for this Court to solve.
To the contrary, it is a choice that must be respected.
The separation of powers forbids this Court to override
what its co -equal branch  has done.  As this Court
recognized in Franklin, to go Petitioner’s route would

12
“harm [the] separation of powers . . . by giving judges
the power to render inutile causes of action authorized
by Congress through a decision that no remedy is
available.” 503 U.S. at 74.
Proper application of the prior construction canon
here requires examination of the state of Bivens law
as of  1988, including any broad and unquestioned
consensus in the courts of appeals.  Only by adhering
to the scope of Bivens when Congress legislated  can
the Court do justice to the decision Congress made
when it passed  the Westfall Act. Absent careful
attention to the scope of what Congress chose to
preserve, judges risk substituting their own
judgments for Congress’s and thereby “arrogating
legislative power.” Hernández, 589 U.S. at 100.
B. Reducing the Carlson “Context” to Its
Specific Facts Would Contravene the
Text of the Westfall Act, Precedent, and
Common Sense.
According to Petitioner, Mr. Watanabe’s claim falls
within a “new context” because his complaint is about
unconstitutionally deficient medical care for a broken
tailbone, not an asthma attack. Pet’r’s Br. 24–29. But
see Abbasi, 582 U.S. at 149 (“Some differences . . . will
be so trivial that they will not suffice to create a new
Bivens context.”). That position cannot be reconciled
with either  the text of the Westfall Act or the
precedent of this Court.
Petitioner’s theory that Congress legislated to
preserve Bivens actions in just three highly specific
factual scenarios is at odds with the broad statutory
language of the Westfall Act. The text of

13
§ 2679(b)(2)(A) preserves an “action  . . . brought for a
violation of the Constitution.” It contains no
exceptions. If Congress meant for the savings clause
to cover only the fact patterns of three Supreme Court
cases, it would have inserted that limitation into the
statute’s text. Cf. FDA v. R.J. Reynolds Vapor Co., 606
U.S. 226, 228  (2025) (“Congress knows how to limit
the scope of a cause of action.”).
In fact, Congress did put these kinds of liability
limits into the statute—just not in the provision
concerning Bivens. The very next section of the FTCA
spells out thirteen exceptions to governmental
liability, including bars on claims regarding federal
employees’ discretionary functions, combatant
activities, Treasury functions, mail delivery, customs
functions, conduct occurring abroad, certain
intentional torts, and more . See 28 U.S.C . § 2680.
Congress could have  limited the savings clause for
claims “brought for a violation of the Constitution” to
only those claims about incarcerated individuals who
died following  unconstitutionally deficient  care for
their asthma (or to other fact patterns in this Court’s
cases). But it did  not. See id.  at §  2679(b)(2)(A).
Congress’s choice must now be respected. See Jama v.
ICE, 543 U.S. 335, 341 (2005)  (“We do not lightly
assume that Congress has omitted from its adopted
text requirements that it nonetheless intends to
apply, and our reluctance is even greater when
Congress has shown elsewhere in the same statute
that it knows how to make such a require ment
manifest.”).
When it legislated on a foundation of this Court’s
precedents including  Carlson, Congress understood

14
the “context” not to concern only cases about asthma
deaths in prison . Congress, and the public, did not
believe that there  was an arbitrary regime in which
the availability of a remedy turns on whether a case
sufficiently resembles the facts of the three cases that
the Supreme Court happened to choose to resolve
between 1971 and 1980. Legal rules do not work like
that, and for good reason: it  is a “basic principle of
justice that like cases should be decided alike.” Martin
v. Franklin Cap. Corp. , 546 U.S. 132, 139 (2005) ; see
also Epic Sys. Corp. v. Lewis, 584 U.S. 497, 510 (2018)
(“The law of precedent teaches that like cases should
generally be treated alike[.]”). And, as for whether two
cases are “like,” no one in Congress, or the public, has
ever understood that question to turn on something as
arbitrary as whether officials deprived a person of
medical care for asthma versus a broken bone.
Petitioner’s position is also at odds with Franklin,
discussed above . In Franklin, no Justice suggested
that when Congress endorse d the Title IX cause of
action that Cannon had previously inferred, it did so
only as to Cannon’s specific fact pattern (a claim of
discrimination in medical school admissions). See 441
U.S. at 680. On the contrary, Franklin had no trouble
concluding that Congress’s decision to permit the
recovery of damages under the previously recognized
cause of action extended to very different
circumstances: a middle school student who had been
sexually assaulted by a teacher. See 503 U.S. at 63.
Franklin shows that when Congress endorses courts’
handiwork, it does not focus on  “trivial” differences
between individual fact patterns. Cf. Abbasi, 582 U.S.
at 149 . Instead, Congress adopts  the underlying

15
principle—the “judicially defined concept” —that
courts have articulated. Davis, 489 U.S. at 813 ; cf.
Cisco Sys. v. Doe, 146 S. Ct. 1882, 1888, 1892 (2026)
(recognizing that Congress, in passing the Alien Tort
Statute, expected it to be applied in three cabined, but
general, categories of tort claims identified by
Blackstone—violation of safe conducts, infringement
of the rights of ambassadors, and piracy).
Restricting Congress’s work to three specific fact
patterns would be an “arrogati[on of] legislative
power,” Hernández, 589 U.S. at 100,  in another way,
too: it would retroactively impose presumptions  on a
Congress that could not have known about them when
it acted. “Although background presumptions can
inform the understanding of a word or phrase, those
presumptions must exist at the time of enactment. We
cannot manufacture a new presumption now and
retroactively impose it on a Congress that acted [more
than a quarter century] ago.” Tanzin, 592 U.S. at 52 .
No court in 1988  required precise factual congruence
with Carlson’s facts as a prerequisite for applying
Carlson’s principle . As Part II demonstrates , the
broad and unquestioned consensus in the courts of
appeals was that Carlson did not create a special rule
for incarcerated asthmatics who died for lack of
medical care, but instead authorized  Eighth
Amendment prison medical care claims as a category.
Today, the  “context” i nquiry of modern Bivens
jurisprudence upholds the separation of powers by
preventing extensions of Bivens to novel
circumstances Congress could not have authorized in
1988. See, e.g. , Abbasi, 582 U.S. at 125, 146
(investigation of terror attacks); Hernández, 589 U.S.

16
at 96 (incidents at the international border) ; Egbert,
596 U.S. at 494 (same). Other post-1988 Bivens cases
likewise have rejected  claims that were unsupported
by a broad and uniform consensus  in 1988, including
cases against federal agencies directly, FDIC v. Meyer,
510 U.S. 471, 484 (1994); against private corporations,
Corr. Servs. Corp. v. Malesko , 534 U.S. 61, 71 (2001) ;
against private contractors, Minneci v. Pollard , 565
U.S. 118, 120 (2012) ; based on a novel theory of
“retaliation for exercising [plaintiff’s] property right,”
Wilkie v. Robbins, 551 U.S. 537, 550 (2007); and where
Congress explicitly foreclosed liability, Hui, 559 U.S.
at 802. Never, however, has the Court announced that
the scope of a Bivens “context” contracts Bivens to less
than what Congress preserved in the Westfall Act.
Petitioner would have this Court do exactly that.
In Petitioner’s hands, the “context” inquiry becomes a
hatchet to lop off whole swaths of Bivens applications
that Congress (and the public) have relied upon. That
flips the separation of powers on its head . Narrowing
the “context” inquiry post-hoc and superimposing it on
the Westfall Act is exactly the type of retrofitting this
Court has unanimously disapproved. Tanzin, 592 U.S.
at 52.
C. The Westfall Act Does Not Permit
Construing the Administrative Remedy
Program To Destroy the Carlson
Context.
Petitioner and the United States are not content
to limit Bivens to the facts of this Court’s three
original Bivens cases. W ith their argument that the
Administrative Remedy Program ( “ARP”) now

17
renders every Carlson claim new, they would go
further and effectively eliminate the entire Carlson
“context.” The United States says the quiet part out
loud, urging this Court to declare that “the class of
viable Carlson claims has become a null set.” Amicus
Br. for U.S. 25; accord, e.g., id. at 3 (“no more Carlson
claims will be viable”).
This position is anathema to the separation of
powers: The government asks the Court to take a red
pen to the text of the Westfall Act, writing into the text
a broad exception that Congress did not enact. Again,
Congress preserved, without exception,
“action[s] . . . brought for a violation of the
Constitution,” 28 U.S.C. § 2679(b)(2)(A); it did not say,
“except for claims arising in federal prison.”
Respecting Congress means respecting what Congress
said, not what the government wishes it had said.
Because the dispositive inquiry is what Congress
directed, Petitioner’s focus on the absence of the ARP
from the Carlson decision, see Pet’r’s Br. 37–38, is
misplaced. Even if the Court did not mention the ARP
in Carlson, Congress certainly knew of the ARP when
it endorsed Carlson in 1988. See Hall v. United States,
566 U.S. 506, 516 (2012)  (“Congress is aware of
existing law when it passes legislation .” ( quoting
Miles v. Apex Marine Corp. , 498 U.S. 19, 32 (1990) )).
And nothing in the text of the Westfall Act suggests
that Congress intended the existence of the ARP to
preclude the availability of the Carlson remedy—
indeed, the text says the opposite. Petitioner (like the
government) asks the Court to read the Westfall Act
against itself  and construe the savings clause as
silently excluding  all Carlson claims. The Court

18
should refuse to engage in such a creative reimagining
of what Congress said. The statute’s text provides the
Court with all it needs. See Hartford Underwriters
Ins. Co. v. Union Planters Bank, N.A. , 530 U.S. 1, 6
(2000) (“Congress says in a statute what it means and
means in a statute what it says there.” (citation
modified)).
Rarely has giving accurate meaning to what
Congress said mattered more . Where lower courts
have ignored Congress and relied on the ARP to
hollow out  Carlson, the toll of these decisions is
measured by life and limb. For instance, the Eleventh
Circuit recently relied on the ARP to reject a Bivens
claim for fatally inadequate medical treatment of
Hepatitis C in prison “even though [the plaintiff’s]
estate could not use the ARP after his death.” Carrin
v. Strong, 182 F.4th 1351, 1354 (11th Cir. 2026) . The
Third Circuit relied on the ARP to reject a Bivens
claim for the failure to treat diabetic blisters that
ultimately required the amputation of the plaintiff’s
toe, even though the “effectiveness” of the ARP was
“dubious.” Muniz v. United States, 149 F.4th 256, 258,
264 (3d Cir. 2025). And the Eleventh Circuit relied on
the ARP in rejecting a Bivens claim for failure to treat
an incarcerated plaintiff’s “severe but ultimately nonlethal physical injuries” even though “the district
court found that he was denied access to the [ARP].”
Johnson v. Terry,  119 F.4th 840, 858 –60 (11th Cir.
2024). None of these outcomes accurately reflect s
congressional will.

19
D. Ignoring the Westfall Act or
Subordinating It to More General
Statutes Would Contravene Precedent,
Statutory Text , and the Separation of
Powers.
No doubt aware that Congress’s preservation of
Bivens actions as they existed in 1988 presents an
obstacle to their desired outcome in this case,
Petitioner and the United States urge this Court to
either ignore or nullify the Westfall Act. Their
arguments should be rejected because they are
contrary to this Court’s precedents, unmoored from
text, and an invitation for this Court to engage in
judicial legislation.
The United States first contends that the Westfall
Act did not “ratify” Bivens but is merely “neutral”
toward it. Amicus Br. for  U.S. 28. If the government
means that the Westfall Act took no action regarding
Bivens, it is profoundly mistaken. As this Court has
explained on four separate occasions, Congress did act
on Bivens via the Westfall Act: Through its “explicit”
statutory text, Hui, 559 U.S. at 807, Congress “left
open claims for constitutional violations,” Tanzin, 592
U.S. at 49 , “expressly  . . . preserving” some Bivens
claims, Smith, 499 U.S. at 173 , by “le[aving] Bivens
where it found it,” Hernández, 589 U.S. at 111 n.9. If,
instead, the government simply means that Congress
did not expand Bivens beyond its 1988 contours, that
is a settled point. See id.  Ultimately, what is clear
from this Court’s repeated discussions is that
Congress did affirmatively act to preserve Bivens. In
keeping with the “utmost deference” owed “to
Congress’ preeminent authority” in determining what

20
causes of action should exist, Egbert, 596 U.S. at 492,
Congress’s enactment of statutory language
preserving Bivens as of 1988 cannot simply be ignored
because the government wishes Congress had done
something else or done nothing at all.
Petitioner and the United States  then attempt to
minimize the Westfall Act by embracing other, more
general congressional enactments regarding prison
litigation (mainly the PLRA) and asking the Court to
infer from these that Congress would not have wanted
Bivens to persist in the prison context.  See Pet’r’s Br.
33–35; Amicus Br. for  U.S. 16–17. But far from
undercutting such claims , the PLRA confirms
Congress’s understanding that Carlson claims would
continue to exist. As Petitioner admits, the PLRA
requires exhaustion via the ARP, and therefore PLRA
exhaustion applies to “federal prisoners,”  Pet’r’s Br.
18, 33—the very people whose remedy in federal court
is a Carlson claim. It would make no sense for
Congress to enact an exhaustion requirement  in the
PLRA that was applicable to Carlson claims if it, in
fact, intended to abolish such claims altogether.
In any event, basic principles of statutory
interpretation show that , at the very least, the
statutes on which Petitioner and the United States
focus did not displace the Westfall Act’s preservation
of Bivens as it existed in 1988. To start, none of these
later statutes said anything about Bivens or otherwise
suggested that damages actions against federal prison
officers should not or did not exist. And Petitioner’s
and the United States’ argument that the PLRA and
other general federal statutes impliedly displaced the
Westfall Act ’s savings clause  cannot come close to

21
demonstrating a “clearly expressed congressional
intention that such a result should follow.”  Epic Sys.
Corp. v. Lewis , 584 U.S. 497, 510 (2018) ( citation
modified). This Court has long maintained a “strong
presumption that repeals by implication are
disfavored and that Congress will specifically address
preexisting law when it wishes to suspend its normal
operations in a later statute. ” Id. (citation modified);
accord, e.g., Dep’t of Agric. v. Kirtz , 601 U.S. 42, 63
(2024). Petitioner and the United States seem to
forget that “t hese rules exist for good reasons ”:
Respect for Congress and respect for the separation of
powers. Epic Sys. Corp. , 584 U.S. at 51 1 (citation
modified). “The courts are not at liberty to pick and
choose among congressional enactments.” Morton v.
Mancari, 417 U.S. 535, 551 (1974).
What is more, this Court “[t]ime and again . . . has
rejected every attempt to deviate from the PLRA’s
textual mandate.” Ross v. Blake , 578 U.S. 632, 633
(2016) (citing examples). The Court’s  “adherence to
the PLRA’s text  . . . applies regardless of whether it
benefits the inmate or the prison,” id. at 640 n.1, and
is required by the separation of powers, because where
“rules are not required by the PLRA,  . . . crafting and
imposing them exceeds the proper limits on the
judicial role.” Jones v. Bock, 549 U.S. 199, 203 (2007);
accord Ross, 578 U.S. at 640 n.1 . Petitioner’s and the
United States’ implied -displacement argument urges
the Court to violate the separation of powers twice
over—first by ignoring the  express preservation of
Bivens remedies in the  Westfall Act and  then by
reading into the PLRA an implied displacement of

22
Carlson remedies that appears nowhere in the PLRA’s
text.
Harmonizing the Westfall Act and the other
statutes cited by Petitioner and the United States is
not difficult: The Westfall Act preserves Bivens as it
existed in 1988, including Carlson. Where such claims
are brought, they are subject to the procedural and
substantive limitations of the PLRA, such as the
exhaustion requirement, 42 U.S.C. § 1997e(a), and the
restriction on recovery for certain types of injuries, id.
§ 1997e(e). And the other statutes Petitioner and the
United States cite provide additional avenues for
oversight without adding to or subtracting from the
Bivens cause of action that the Westfall Act preserves.
“Because [the Court] can easily read Congress’s
statutes to work in harmony, that is where [its] duty
lies.” Epic Sys. Corp., 584 U.S. at 525.
The Court’s previous references to  the PLRA
when deciding Bivens cases do not counsel a different
result. Abbasi contrasted Congress’s failure to provide
a damages remedy for Fifth Amendment detention
claims with Congress’s related activity in the field  of
prison litigation . See 582 U.S. at 148 –49. But the
Court’s consideration of the PLRA there concerned a
circumstance where Congress had been silent
regarding the cause of action, not a circumstance
where Congress had acted to preserve what had
already been established.  And Goldey v. Fields , 606
U.S. 942, 944 (2025)  (per curiam), briefly cited that
passage from Abbasi without elaboration. The Court
has never considered whether the PLRA displaces the
Westfall Act’s “explicit” statutory text, Hui, 559 U.S.
at 807—text that “left open claims for constitutional

23
violations,” Tanzin, 592 U.S. at 49 , and thereby
“expressly . . . preserv[ed]” some Bivens claims,
Smith, 499 U.S. at 173.
Statutory interpretation is not a choose-your-ownadventure novel  or “an exercise in looking over a
crowd and picking out your friends.” Exxon Mobil
Corp. v. Allapattah Servs., Inc. , 545 U.S. 546, 568
(2005) (citation modified). Petitioner provides no basis
to disregard the Westfall Act or to abandon the Court’s
previous understanding that Congress “left Bivens
where it found it” in 1988, Hernández, 589 U.S. at 111
n.9. Like the PLRA, the Westfall Act must be
respected, not ignored . To do otherwise would be to
flout the clear limits of the judicial role.  “Allowing
judges to pick and choose between statutes risks
transforming them from expounders of what the law
is into policymakers choosing what the law should be.”
Epic Sys. Corp., 584 U.S. at 511.
II. IN 1988, THE COURTS OF APPEALS
UNIFORMLY APPLIED  BIVENS TO ANY
EIGHTH AMENDMENT CLAIM FOR
INADEQUATE PRISON MEDICAL CARE.
As established above, the task before the Court is
to determine the scope of the Bivens cause of action
that Congress preserved in 1988 via the Westfall Act.
Under the prior construction canon, Mr. Watanabe’s
claim should be allowed, because it unquestionably
would have been allowed in 1988.  At that time ,
Carlson was well-understood to apply generally to
prisoners’ claims under the Eighth Amendment for
inadequate prison medical care.

24
In 1988, this Court’s Bivens inquiry did not rely
on precise factual congruence with prior Bivens cases.
Instead, to determine whether a Bivens cause of action
was available, the Court looked to whether there were
“special factors counselling hesitation in the absence
of affirmative action by Congress” and whether
“Congress has provided an alternative remedy.”
Carlson, 446 U.S. at 18 (citation modified) ; accord
McCarthy v. Madigan, 503 U.S. 140, 151 (1992)  (“We
have recognized that a Bivens remedy does not lie in
two situations: (1) where Congress has provided an
equally effective alternative remedy and declared it to
be a substitute for recovery under the Constitution,
and (2) where, in the absence of affirmative action by
Congress, special factors counsel hesitation.”); United
States v. Stanley, 483 U.S. 669, 678 (1987) (explaining
that “‘special factors counselling hesitation’ or an
‘explicit congressional declaration’ that another
remedy is exclusive would bar” a Bivens action); see
also Schweiker v. Chilicky , 487 U.S. 412, 423 (1988)
(Court considers “special factors ,” including “ [w]hen
the design of a Government program suggests that
Congress has provided what it considers adequate
remedial mechanisms for constitutional violations”);
Chappell v. Wallace , 462 U.S. 296, 304 (1983)
(presence of “special factors” doomed claim); Bush v.
Lucas, 462 U.S. 367, 378 (1983)  (Court considers
congressional intent reflected in any “alternative
remedy” it provided, along with “special factors”).
Where an existing category of Bivens claims had been
recognized, i n no case did the Court compare the
precise facts of a proposed Bivens claim to the precise
facts of its prior cases and reject  that proposed claim
if there was not a close match.

25
Consistent with this Court’s  approach, every
circuit court that considered, prior to the Westfall
Act’s passage, whether Bivens applied to an  Eighth
Amendment prison medical-care claim, concluded
that it did , notwithstanding differences from the
specific facts of Carlson (a failure to treat asthma
resulting in the plaintiff’s death). See Smith-Bey v.
Hosp. Adm ’r, 841 F.2d 751, 759 –60 (7th Cir. 1988)
(reversing dismissal of Eighth Amendment Bivens
claim where plaintiff was given ice packs “for a wound
that was bleeding ‘profusely’” and “for a broken nose
that apparently had a piece of cartilage protruding
from the skin”); Muhammad v. Carlson, 739 F.2d 122,
123, 126 (3d Cir. 1984)  (vacating dismissal of Eighth
Amendment Bivens claim regarding prison
physician’s treatment of back injury); Goar v. Civiletti,
688 F.2d 27, 28 –29 (6th Cir. 1982)  (reversing
dismissal of Eighth Amendment Bivens claim where
plaintiff “suffered loss of blood from a head wound, a
neck and jaw injury, for which he received inadequate
medical treatment”); Gillespie v. Civiletti , 629 F.2d
637, 639, 642 (9th Cir. 1980)  (reversing dismissal of
Eighth Amendment Bivens claim regarding months -
long denial of medical care that led to “a severe skin
disease, mental depression, abnormal emotional
behavior, and severe emotional distress”).  It did not
matter in these cases that plaintiffs did not face
“damages or nothing” situations, contra Pet’r’s Br. 18
(seeking to distinguish Carlson on this basis); indeed,
the plaintiff in Goar did seek injunctive relief, see 688
F.2d at 28, and given that none of the plaintiffs in
these cases died, they all could have sought injunctive
relief during the period of deficient medical care.

26
The appellate consensus also reveals that , at the
time Congress passed the Westfall Act, the Bureau of
Prisons’ ARP  was not a viable basis to defeat a n
Eighth Amendment Bivens claim for inadequate
medical care in prison.  No court prior to the Westfall
Act’s passage denied the existence of an Eighth
Amendment prison medical care claim  under Bivens
based on the availability of an internal grievance
process. Indeed, up to that point, the only precedential
federal appellate decisions to discuss the ARP in
connection with Bivens did so to address the then -
ongoing debate over whether Bivens plaintiffs were
required to exhaust administrative remedies before
proceeding with their Bivens claims—not to foreclose
the existence of a Bivens claim entirely. Compare
Hessbrook v. Lennon , 777 F.2d 999, 1003 –04, 1007
(5th Cir. 1985) (discussing ARP in holding that FTCA
exhaustion was required but noting that district court
could stay Bivens claim pending exhaustion), and
Brice v. Day , 604 F.2d 664, 667 –68 (10th Cir. 1979)
(requiring exhaustion but indicating that that courts
“may order [such cases] referred to the prison officials
for an administrative review before the trial court
considers them further ” (emphasis added)), with
Muhammad, 739 F.2d at 124–25 (concluding that
BOP grievance process did not license courts to create
exhaustion requirement where Congress had not) ,
and Goar , 688 F.2d at 28 –29 (citing limitations on
ARP as reason that no exhaustion was required).2

2 The ARP was also mentioned in one unpublished appellate
decision about a Bivens claim for obstructing access to the ARP
itself. Gillan v. Edwards , 780 F.2d 1021 (6th Cir.

27
As this history demonstrates, the notion that a
prison grievance process negated the existence of a
Bivens claim would have been entirely foreign to
Congress when it enacted the Westfall Act. Thus, to
conclude that the Westfall Act somehow incorporated
the thoroughly modern contention that the ARP
defeats Bivens claims—without any statutory text or
then-extant precedent saying so —would require the
Court to take the inappropriate step of “retroactively
impos[ing]” a new presumption “on a Congress that
acted [more than a quarter-century] ago.” Tanzin, 592
U.S. at 52.
In sum, there is no question that when Congress
explicitly preserved an action “brought for a violation
of the Constitution of the United States ,” 28 U.S.C.
§ 2679(b)(2)(A), that phrase would have been well
understood to encompass Eighth Amendment Bivens
claims for unconstitutionally deficient prison medical
care generally, not just claims about a prison’s fatal
failure to treat asthma . Nor would the ARP have
posed a bar to such claims . The separation of powers
requires that the “new context” test be applied to
conform to the expectations of Congress, not the other
way around. The Court should affirm the Ninth
Circuit’s holding and conclude that Mr. Watanabe’s
claim falls easily within the Carlson “context.”

1985) (unpublished table decision). Four years after the Westfall
Act passed, this Court resolved the circuit split over exhaustion,
holding that it was not required. McCarthy, 503 U.S. at 149–52.
Congress effectively overruled McCarthy via the PLRA’s
imposition of a stricter exhaustion requirement. See Woodford v.
Ngo, 548 U.S. 81, 85 (2006).

28
CONCLUSION
For these reasons, and for those advanced by
Respondent, the judgment below should be affirmed.
